## How they got there
Paris Saint-Germain secured the title by beating Arsenal on penalties in the final after a 1-1 draw, with the shootout ending 4-3. Their path to the summit was defined by elite offensive metrics, as they outperformed 97% of that season's teams in Attacks per game and 100% in Passes per game. Additionally, they ranked higher than 89% of their peers in Goal difference per game, showcasing a dominant statistical profile throughout the knockout stages.

## Would the model have picked them?
Although the club achieved a 16.1% probability of reaching the final—nearly double the 8.3% base rate for a random knockout team—their rank of 4 among all participants suggests the model did not select them as a primary favorite. The algorithm's expected stage figure of 1.73 places their projected outcome nearest to the quarter-finals, indicating that despite the high probability relative to the average, the system viewed them as a leading contender rather than a top-two lock.

## Weak spots
The team's least impressive metrics were Long passes (% of passes), where they beat only 8% of teams, and Distance covered per game (km), at 28%. While these figures represent their lowest relative performance, the model also marked down Shots per game despite the club ranking in the top 100% for that stat. This discrepancy highlights a statistical association where high shot volume was viewed negatively by the algorithm's knockout stage expectations.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Better than this %' figures say how many teams the club beat on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where beating a team means having the lower value. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat drove, propelled, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Write plain markdown without tables.
